tagline.text: A pine-shaded camping island off Padre Burgos, one night from Manila

location.label: Location
location.text: Off Marao, Padre Burgos, Quezon, on Tayabas Bay

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (per person, one night of camping, excluding Manila transport)

children.text: Dampalitan Island is a small island in Tayabas Bay off Padre Burgos, Quezon, known as a camping spot with a white-sand beach and a grove of agoho (sea pine) trees. With no electricity, the night sky is clear, and it pairs well with Borawan Island for a one-night trip from Manila.

Dampalitan Island lies off the Marao area of Padre Burgos, Quezon, on the northern edge of Tayabas Bay. Behind a long, wide stretch of off-white sand stand rows of agoho (sea pine) and coconut palms, giving it an unusually calm feel even among tropical beaches. Unlike nearby Borawan Island in Padre Burgos, which fills with people coming for photos, Dampalitan is mostly visited by campers who stay the night, so it is relatively quiet.

Camping is the main reason the island became popular. There is no electricity, so it gets truly dark after sunset, and on clear nights the stars pour out. Accounts also say that, unlike Anawangin Cove in Zambales, bonfires are allowed here, so many people grill meat over a fire on the beach. Rules can change, though, so check with the caretaker on site first. One side of the beach has a rocky area where you can walk among the reef rocks at low tide, and beyond the cliff there is said to be a quiet little cove ringed by mangroves.
The island is about
10~15 minutes

by boat from Padre Burgos town. Take a bus from Manila to Lucena, change to a bus toward Unisan, get off in Padre Burgos, and take a tricycle to the boat landing. The whole trip takes roughly half a day, so with an early bus you can arrive around midday on the first day, pitch your tent, and watch the sunset. A 2021 GMA News report described it as two to three hours from Manila, but by public transport it is more realistic to allow 5 to 6 hours including transfers and waiting.

Facilities are basic. Many accounts mention a few shared toilets and showers taken with a pail and dipper. There is no store or restaurant, so bring your own food and drinking water or buy water from island residents. In return, that inconvenience gives a clear sense of leaving the city behind. Swim only inside the designated area enclosed by a net against jellyfish, and go expecting to relax on the beach, stargaze and sit by a bonfire rather than to snorkel. Dampalitan is commonly combined with Borawan Island and Puting Buhangin in a day or overnight island-hopping route. Hiring a boat for just Borawan and Dampalitan costs less, and adding Puting Buhangin raises the price. Fees and boat rates differ by source and by year, so use the ranges in the cost table below as a guide and confirm current amounts with the local government unit (LGU) or your boatman before you go.

The main beach is a long, wide stretch of off-white sand backed by rows of agoho (sea pine) and coconut palms. The shade means there is room to pitch a tent even at midday, and you can hear the wind in the pine needles.
With no electricity on the island, it gets very dark after sunset and the stars show well. A stargazing app downloaded in advance adds to the fun, and be sure to bring a flashlight and a power bank.

Accounts say bonfires are allowed here, unlike at Anawangin. One account mentions locals selling firewood, and another says the island caretaker lent a grill. When you use fire, follow the caretaker's instructions and leave no trash or ashes behind.

One side of the beach has a rocky area where, in the late afternoon when the water drops, you can walk among reef rocks and pools, and it is said to be good for sunset photos. Reviews mention slippery footing and sea urchins, so wear sandals or water shoes.

blocks.title: A quiet cove ringed by mangroves

children.text: Walking past the cliff to the right of the main beach is said to lead to a quiet sandy cove ringed by mangroves. It is good for a stroll with few people around, but there are many rocks, so check the tide and your footwear.

blocks.title: Swimming area with a jellyfish net

children.text: The island has a designated swimming area enclosed by a net to keep out jellyfish. One review describes someone stung after swimming out through the opening in the net, so swim only inside the net.

blocks.title: Hopping with Borawan and Puting Buhangin

children.text: From the same Aplaya landing, one boat can take you around Borawan, Dampalitan and Puting Buhangin. Itineraries suggest visiting Borawan early before it gets crowded, or sleeping on Dampalitan and moving on to Borawan the next morning.

Agree the boat schedule with your boatman in advance and confirm the pick-up time. If the sea is rough, you may not be able to reach far islands such as Puting Buhangin.

children.text: A tricycle from in front of QCRB Bank to the Aplaya landing takes about
15 minutes
. Tell the driver you are going to Borawan or Dampalitan.
Boarding from the shore near Borawan Island Resort or Tamarind Tree Resort (Barangay Basiao) is also described.
A 2021 GMA News report said boats leave from Laguimanoc Port, so confirm the departure port locally.
The boat ride from the landing to Dampalitan takes about
10~15 minutes
Many sources give about
(for 8 people) for a boat covering Borawan, Dampalitan and Puting Buhangin, and some give about
for Borawan and Dampalitan only.
If the sea is rough you may not reach the far islands, so check the weather and whether boats are running.
Rates are said to be negotiable, and the boat fare is the same even for one passenger, so it pays to gather a group and split it.
If driving, the route runs through Lucena to Padre Burgos. Check the travel time and parking availability locally and on a map app.
Leave the car near the landing and take the boat. Confirm parking fees locally.
The dry season from November to May, when the sea is calm and the sky clear, is the best time for Dampalitan. For stargazing, December to April, when there is less cloud, is better.

June to October brings heavy rain and typhoon influence, and a review noted plenty of cloud even in late October. In 2014 Typhoon Glenda (international name Rammasun) damaged the island's cottages, so always check the weather forecast before you leave.
Jellyfish are said to appear often in the summer months of March to May. Swim only inside the netted area, and avoid holidays and weekends when crowds arrive; weekdays are quieter.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.

Tent camping is the basic way to stay on the island. Some reports say local boatmen rent out tents, and there are a few cottages on the beach, but they were damaged by a typhoon in 2014, so confirm their current condition locally. Pitch your tent in the pine shade near the beach, and avoid the line the water reaches at high tide.

There is no restaurant on the island, so bring rice, meat, vegetables, snacks, ice and drinking water from the town market or supermarket. Water is also sold by the container on the island, but supplies are limited, so bring plenty. On the mainland side there are places to stay such as Tamarind Tree Resort and Villa Anita Resort, and if camping on the island is not for you, you can sleep on the mainland and visit as a day trip. Room rates and contact details change, so check before booking.
Take an early bus and arrive around midday, and you will have plenty of time to pitch your tent. Check the schedule at your Manila terminal before leaving.
Reviews say there is no ATM in Padre Burgos town. Bring enough cash.
It gets very dark after sunset, so use the toilet before dusk and bring a headlamp and a power bank.
Reviews mention many mosquitoes, so bring insect repellent. A mat or tarp to put under your tent is useful.
There are no trash bins on the island, so take all your garbage out with you. Bring plenty of plastic bags.
Buying a packed meal in town (about ₱30 in one account) saves you worrying about food on the island.
Check that the boat has life vests before boarding. Reviews say some small boats do not have them.
Local requirements may apply on arrival. In 2021 a barangay health certificate was required, so check the latest guidance.
The sun is strong, so bring a hat, sunscreen and long sleeves.
Jellyfish often appear along this coast, so swim only in the netted swimming area, and since some reviews warn of dangerous jellyfish, get first aid locally immediately if you are stung.
Swim only inside the net. One review describes someone stung after going out through the opening in the net.
Reviews mention sea urchins on the rocks and in shallow water, so wear water shoes or sandals.
There is no electricity, toilets are few and showers use a pail. Take care moving around after dark.
Prices differ widely between sources, so confirm the total and the pick-up time before boarding the boat.
During typhoon season or on rough days boats may be cancelled, so leave room in your schedule.
Entry rules (health certificate, reservations, capacity limits) can change, so check the latest announcements from the Padre Burgos LGU.
